title: Why Does God Let Children Suffer?
excerpt: The suffering of children is the hardest form of the hardest question, and the Bible gives it lament, a cross and a promise where we wanted an explanation.
body:
There is a floor in most large hospitals where the chairs in the waiting room are small and the murals on the walls are bright, and where parents learn words they never wanted to know. There are graves with a single year on the stone. There are houses where a child is afraid of the person who was supposed to keep her safe. Anyone who has stood near one of these places knows that the usual arguments about God and evil get very quiet there.

Adults who suffer have at least lived long enough to sin, to choose, to grow, to make some sense of pain. A sick three-year-old has done none of that. So of all the forms the problem of evil takes, this one has the least room in it for an answer, and it's the one the skeptic is most right to press.

If you're grieving as you read this, you don't have to resolve any of it before you're allowed to pray. Bring the question to God in whatever words you have; the psalms give you permission. Bring it to a person too, a friend or a pastor who will sit with you. If you have started to wonder whether you want to go on living, reach out today: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This essay can't counsel you, but [Find Help](/help) has other lines you can call and a page for grief.

What follows is an argument, and an argument is the wrong thing for the worst week of a life. It is written for the months and years after, and for the person who watches from outside and wonders how anyone goes on believing.

## Ivan's Question

Nobody has put the case better than a Christian novelist did. Fyodor Dostoevsky finished *The Brothers Karamazov* in 1880. Two years earlier his own son, a boy not yet three named Alyosha, had died. In the novel the believing brother carries that name, and the unbelieving brother, Ivan, is given the strongest speech in the book.

Ivan has been collecting stories of cruelty to children from the newspapers. He tells them to his brother one after another, and then he explains why he has kept to children. With adults, he says, there is guilt mixed in, and room to argue. With children there is not. "If all must suffer to pay for the eternal harmony, what have children to do with it, tell me, please?"

What makes Ivan so hard to answer is that he doesn't deny the ending Christians hope for. He grants it. He allows that a day may come when everything is explained and every creature praises God, when even a mother embraces the man who killed her child. And he refuses it in advance: "I renounce the higher harmony altogether." He says that "too high a price is asked for harmony; it's beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it." He would rather keep his anger, he says, "even if I were wrong."

Then he turns the question on his brother. Suppose you were building a world whose purpose was to make everyone happy in the end, and it could only be done by torturing one small child to death. Would you agree to be the architect? Alyosha, the novice from the monastery, answers quietly: "No, I wouldn't consent."

That exchange should be read slowly by anyone who wants to defend God. The believer in the story does not win the argument. He agrees with the premise. A faith that can't feel the force of Ivan's refusal has not understood the question, and it will say foolish things at funerals.

## The Answers, and Where Each One Stops

Christians and other believers in God have not been silent since, and their answers deserve their full strength.

The first is freedom. A world of creatures who can love is a world of creatures who can refuse to, and much of what children suffer is done to them by people. War, neglect, the hand raised in anger: none of it is an act of God in the sense the insurance forms mean. A God who stopped every cruel act before it landed would have made puppets. This answer explains a great deal of the world's pain. It does not explain a tumor.

The second is that God is forming souls. Courage, patience and compassion grow only where something is at stake, and a world without danger would be a world without saints. There is truth in this for the adult who suffers, and sometimes for those who love a suffering child. It has nothing to say to the child who dies at two, who was not here long enough to be formed by anything.

The third is that God rules over all things and brings good from evil that he does not explain. Joseph could say to the brothers who sold him, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Many Christians rest here, and it is a real place to rest: nothing that happens is outside his hands, and his purposes are wiser than ours. Others, who believe just as firmly in God's rule, say that he permits such things without willing them. Either way this answer faces Ivan directly, because Ivan's whole protest is against a good purchased with a child's pain. The Christian who gives this answer has to give it as Joseph did, about his own suffering and after the fact, and never as a ruling on someone else's child.

The fourth is the limit of our sight. If there is a God, his reasons are not the kind of thing we should expect to see from inside one afternoon of history. The philosophers who make this case are careful, and their point is sound as far as it reaches: not seeing a reason is weak evidence that there is none. But it is a defense of God's possible reasons. It tells a mother nothing she can hold.

The fifth is not an explanation at all. It is the conclusion Ivan's unbelieving readers draw, and it has its own strength. There is no God, the world is not arranged for anyone, and children get sick because cells divide badly. This asks nothing to be reconciled. Its cost is that the protest loses its footing along with God. If the universe is indifferent, a child's death is very sad and breaks no promise, since none was made. Ivan's rage assumes that the world owes children better, and it is hard to say who owes it.

Each of these sees something. None of them is equal to one small bed in one hospital room, and the people who thought longest about them have usually said so. Every answer on this list works at the scale of the whole world. Children suffer one at a time.

## What the Bible Does Not Say

It is worth noticing how little of this the Bible attempts.

It never explains why a particular child suffers. Job's ten children die in a single afternoon when "a great wind came across the wilderness" and brought the house down on them (Job 1:19). The reader is shown a scene in heaven. Job never is. His friends supply what God withholds, a theory in which suffering is always earned, and at the end God says to them, "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The man who shouted at God was nearer the truth than the men who explained him.

Jesus was asked the question in the form people still ask it. His disciples saw a man blind from birth and wanted to know whose fault it was: "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" (John 9:2). He refused both choices. He would not trace a child's condition to a parent's sin, and he gave no general theory in its place. A parent who lies awake asking what sin of theirs brought this on their child has heard Jesus refuse that question.

Nor does the Bible say that the suffering of children is good, or secretly a gift, or that God needed another angel. It says the opposite, in its own way of saying things. It weeps.

## What the Bible Does Say

The Bible does not look away from suffering children, and that is the first thing to see. Pharaoh orders Hebrew boys thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22). The poet of Lamentations walks through a starving city and writes that "infants and babies faint in the streets," that their life "is poured out on their mothers' bosom" (Lamentations 2:11–12). Jeremiah hears the mother of the nation crying over the exiles: "Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more" (Jeremiah 31:15).

Matthew puts that verse in the Christmas story. When Herod's soldiers kill the little boys of Bethlehem, the Gospel does not explain it, soften it, or say it served a purpose. It quotes Jeremiah and lets Rachel refuse comfort (Matthew 2:18). The birth of Christ is told with the sound of mothers wailing in it. Whatever Christianity is, it isn't a story that needs children's suffering kept out of sight.

Second, the Bible gives sufferers words that are not polite. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). The prophet Habakkuk asks God, "Why do you make me see iniquity, and why do you idly look at wrong?" (Habakkuk 1:3). These are prayers, kept in the book on purpose. They mean that a parent's anger at God is not unbelief. It is one of the oldest ways of believing, and it is the way Job was commended for.

Third, the Bible shows what God is like toward children when he comes within reach of them. When the disciples tried to keep children away, Jesus "was indignant" and said, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14). He said that anyone who leads one of these little ones into sin would be better off thrown into the sea with a millstone around his neck (Matthew 18:6). A father came to him saying his little girl was dying, and Jesus went, and took her by the hand, and said, "Little girl, I say to you, arise" (Mark 5:41).

The limit has to be stated here too. He raised that girl, and a widow's son, and he did not raise every child who died in Galilee that year. The Gospels present those moments as signs of where things are going. They do not present them as a policy, and no one was promised that his prayer for his own child would be answered the same way. The church has done great harm by suggesting otherwise.

## What We Have Said Instead

We have not kept the Bible's restraint. We have told parents that their child's death was God's will in a tone that made God sound like the one who did it. We have told them it happened for a reason, as though we knew the reason. Some of us have told them their faith was too small, which is the cruelty of Job's friends in modern dress.

And there is a worse thing. Some of the children who suffered were harmed inside our own churches, by people we trusted, and when they spoke we protected the institution. A church that wants to talk about why God permits the suffering of children has to remember that it has sometimes been the cause, and that Jesus' sentence about the millstone was spoken to disciples. If that was done to you, or is being done to a child you know, tell someone you trust. If you need someone sooner, [Find Help](/help) lists hotlines for abuse and sexual assault.

## The One Who Can Forgive

Ivan asks whether there is anyone in the whole world who would have the right to forgive what is done to children. He thinks the mother has no such right, and that no future harmony can supply it. It is the best question in the chapter. Alyosha's answer is the only one he has: "But there is a Being and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and everything."

That is not an explanation either, and Dostoevsky knew it. It changes who is being asked. The Christian claim is that God did not design a world of pain from a safe distance and send others to live in it. The church confesses that the eternal Son became a child, was hunted by Herod as an infant, grew up, and was tortured to death while his mother watched. Simeon had warned her when he was a baby that "a sword will pierce through your own soul also" (Luke 2:35). Paul says that God "did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). On the cross that Son prayed a psalm of abandonment: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

None of this tells a parent why. It does mean that when a parent brings that anger to God, it is brought to a God who knows from the inside what it is to suffer, and what it is to give up a son. The architect in Ivan's question is not standing outside the building. He is under it.

And Christians confess that he rose. If that is true, then the suffering of children is not woven into the final design of things, as Ivan feared it would be. It is an enemy, and it is to be undone. Isaiah saw a world in which "No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days" (Isaiah 65:20). John saw God himself bending down: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore" (Revelation 21:4). Ivan returns his ticket because he can't accept a harmony built on a child's tears. The Bible's last picture is of God's own hand on those tears, one face at a time.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

The church confesses that God is good, that he made all things and rules them, and that he is not the author of evil. It confesses that suffering and death are real evils and are not illusions or lessons in disguise. It confesses that the Son of God suffered and died and was raised, and that he will come to judge and to make all things new. These belong to the faith itself.

How God's rule stands to the evil he does not prevent is a question on which churches that share those confessions have differed for centuries, some saying he ordains it for ends we cannot see and others that he permits it. That is a second-order matter, and no one should break fellowship over it.

Why this child suffered, and not another, is not given to anyone. "The secret things belong to the LORD our God" (Deuteronomy 29:29). A person who claims to know has stopped speaking for the Bible.

The death of a child breaks the order of things, and no sentence makes it make sense, so be wary of anyone who offers one. Find other parents who have buried a child; they can sit with you as others can't. If this question has turned toward your own life, please call or text 988 now.

A skeptic who reads this far will notice that the question in the title was not answered. It wasn't. Job did not get an answer, and Rachel is still refusing to be comforted in the second chapter of the New Testament. What the Bible gives is a God who let that refusal stand in his own book, who came as a child into a world that kills children, and who has promised to end it.

Whether that promise is true can't be settled at a bedside. It rests on whether a grave outside Jerusalem was empty. Until the promise is kept, the question stays open. In John's vision even the martyrs in heaven are still asking it. Their prayer begins, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long" (Revelation 6:10).

*"Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more."* (Jeremiah 31:15)

*"He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."* (Revelation 21:4)
